data.narrative: The student executed a disciplined, hypothesis-driven debugging loop: identified concurrency as the likely trigger, disproved alternative explanations with controlled tests, and reproduced failures under a fixed concurrent workload before and after each change. They traced two related race classes: a loud check-then-act duplicate-key failure and a silent timestamp correctness issue under concurrent upserts. The final design uses a permanent atomic upsert with GREATEST to preserve both correctness and monotonic timestamp semantics, verified by repeated concurrent runs and count/timestamp checks.

strengths: Hypothesis-driven elimination: disproved incorrect causes with reproducible evidence before committing to fixes.
High-quality reproduction practice: maintained the same controlled concurrent workload across before/after comparisons.
Root-cause depth: addressed both loud failure (500/unique violation) and silent correctness risk (timestamp semantics under concurrency).
Durable fix selection: adopted atomic ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE with GREATEST to prevent timestamp regression while preserving count correctness.
data.recommendation: Carry this same deterministic-repro discipline into performance debugging by adding latency budgets and profiler traces to separate correctness from throughput bottlenecks early.
